constitution = the basic set of laws that says how a country is governed
parliament = the elected body that makes a country's laws
local government = the councils and officials who run towns, cities and regions
judiciary = the system of courts and judges in a country
legislature = the branch of government that writes and passes laws
executive power = the branch of government that puts laws into practice
head of state = the official who represents a country, such as a president or monarch
cabinet = the group of senior ministers who run government departments
civil service = the professional officials who administer the state, not elected politicians
civil servant = a person employed by the state to run public administration
pass a bill = to approve a proposed law in parliament
amendment = a change made to a law or a proposed law
rule of law = the principle that everyone, including the government, is bound by the law
separation of powers = dividing state power between legislature, executive and judiciary
democracy = a system in which citizens choose their leaders in free elections
dictatorship = rule by one person or group who hold power by force, not free choice
authoritarian regime = a government that demands obedience and limits political freedom
constitutional monarchy = a system with a king or queen whose powers are limited by law
republic = a state whose head is elected or appointed, not a hereditary monarch
sovereignty = the right of a state to govern itself without outside control
constituency = a district whose voters elect a representative
member of parliament = a person elected to sit in parliament
upper house = the second chamber of a parliament, such as a senate
lower house = the main elected chamber of a parliament
municipality = a town or district with its own local government
councillor = an elected member of a local council
bureaucracy = a system of administration with many official rules and procedures
red tape = official rules that seem unnecessary and delay action
watchdog organisation = a body that monitors institutions and reports abuse
public administration = the organisation and work of government offices and services
checks and balances = rules that stop any one branch of government becoming too powerful
act of parliament = a law that has been passed by parliament and come into force
electorate = all the people who are entitled to vote
turnout = the percentage of eligible voters who actually vote
coalition = an alliance of parties that govern together
referendum = a nationwide vote in which citizens decide a specific question
lobbying = trying to influence politicians and officials on behalf of a group
left-wing = supporting greater social equality and a larger role for the state
right-wing = supporting tradition, lower taxes or a smaller role for the state
centre-ground = moderate political positions between left and right
general election = a nationwide election to choose a new parliament
proportional representation = an electoral system in which seats match the share of votes
manifesto = a public statement of a party's policies before an election
populism = politics that claims to speak for ordinary people against elites
nationalism = a political belief that puts one's nation first, sometimes at others' expense
swing voter = a voter who is not loyal to one party and can decide an election
secret ballot = a vote in which nobody can see how you chose
hung parliament = a parliament in which no party has an overall majority
opposition = the parties not in government, who criticise those in power
minority government = a government that does not have a majority of seats
vote of no confidence = a parliamentary vote to remove the government from office
grassroots = ordinary members of a party or movement, not its leaders
political spectrum = the range of political views from left to right
incumbent = the person or party currently holding office
suffrage = the right to vote in elections
disenfranchised = deprived of the right to vote
opinion poll = a survey of people's views, often on parties or policies
landslide victory = an election win by a very large margin
abstain = to formally decline to vote for or against a motion
electoral fraud = illegal interference with the process of an election
accountability = the duty of those in power to explain and justify their actions
corruption = dishonest use of power for private gain, such as taking bribes
bribery = offering or taking money or gifts to influence an official decision
nepotism = giving jobs or favours to relatives rather than on merit
freedom of information = the right to see official documents held by the state
propaganda = information spread to promote a political cause, often one-sided
prosecute = to bring a criminal case against someone in court
defendant = the person accused of a crime or sued in a civil case
community service = unpaid work for the community, given as a punishment
petty crime = relatively minor offences such as shoplifting or vandalism
organised crime = crime planned and carried out by structured groups
prosecutor = the lawyer who presents the case against the accused
defence lawyer = the lawyer who represents the person accused of a crime
jury = a group of citizens who decide if the accused is guilty
verdict = the decision of a jury or court at the end of a trial
acquit = to formally find that someone is not guilty
convict = to find someone guilty of a crime
life imprisonment = a prison sentence for the rest of a person's life
probation = a sentence served in the community under supervision instead of prison
parole = early release from prison under conditions
bail = money paid as a guarantee that an accused person will return to court
warrant = an official document allowing the police to arrest someone or search a place
testimony = a formal statement given as evidence in court
presumption of innocence = the principle that a person is innocent until proved guilty
fair trial = a hearing that is independent, public and respects the rights of both sides
appeal = a request to a higher court to review a decision
white-collar crime = non-violent crime committed by people in business or public office
money laundering = hiding the origin of money obtained from crime
embezzlement = stealing money that you were trusted to look after
human trafficking = the illegal trade in people for exploitation
manslaughter = killing someone without the intent required for murder
arson = the crime of deliberately setting fire to property
perjury = the crime of lying in court after swearing to tell the truth
rehabilitation of offenders = helping people who have committed crimes to return to honest life
recidivism = the tendency of former prisoners to commit further crimes
miscarriage of justice = a serious failure of the legal system, such as convicting an innocent person
deterrent = something that discourages people from committing a crime
law enforcement = the police and other agencies that make sure laws are obeyed
inflation = a general rise in prices that reduces the value of money
recession = a period when the economy shrinks for a significant time
GDP = the total value of goods and services produced in a country
welfare state = a system in which the state provides healthcare, education and support for those in need
tax evasion = illegally hiding income or profits to avoid paying tax
tax avoidance = using legal loopholes to pay as little tax as possible
income tax = a tax paid on money you earn from work or investments
public spending = money the government spends on services and investment
budget deficit = the amount by which government spending exceeds income
national debt = the total amount a government owes
austerity = government policy of cutting spending to reduce debt
unemployment rate = the percentage of the workforce without a job and seeking one
means-tested benefit = state help given only if your income is below a limit
income inequality = large gaps between what rich and poor people earn
universal basic income = a regular sum paid by the state to every citizen
unemployment benefit = money paid by the state to people who have lost their jobs
means-tested = available only if your income and savings are below a set level
privatisation = selling a state-owned company or service to private owners
nationalisation = bringing a private company or sector under state ownership
austerity measures = government cuts in spending to reduce a budget deficit
state-owned = owned and controlled by the government
subsidy = money given by the state to keep prices down or support an industry
cost of living = the amount of money needed for basic everyday expenses
economic growth = an increase in the amount of goods and services an economy produces
black market = illegal trade in goods or currencies that are banned or rationed
fiscal policy = government decisions on tax and public spending
monetary policy = how a central bank controls money supply and borrowing costs
secular = not connected with religion; keeping religion out of public institutions
poverty = the state of not having enough money for a decent standard of living
inequality = an unfair difference in wealth, rights or opportunities
discrimination = unfair treatment of people because of who they are
civil rights = the rights of citizens to political and social freedom and equality
NGO = a non-governmental organisation that works independently of the state
volunteering = giving your time unpaid to help other people or a cause
charity = an organisation that helps people in need; the act of giving that help
social exclusion = being shut out of the opportunities most people take for granted
social mobility = the ability to move up (or down) the income and class scale
gender equality = equal rights and opportunities for women and men
equal opportunities = the principle that people should compete on a fair basis, without bias
hate crime = a crime motivated by hostility towards a person's identity
xenophobia = dislike or fear of people from other countries
social cohesion = the sense of solidarity and trust that holds a community together
ageing population = a situation in which the average age of people in a country is rising
birth rate = the number of live births per thousand people in a year
demographic change = a shift in the size or structure of a population
brain drain = the emigration of highly skilled people to other countries
wealth gap = the difference between the richest and the poorest in a society
underprivileged = not enjoying the standard of living or rights that most people have
marginalised = pushed to the edge of society and ignored by those in power
civil society = organisations and citizens acting independently of the state and the market
religious minority = a faith group that is smaller than the main religion in a country
interfaith = involving people of different religions working or talking together
civic engagement = citizens taking part in public life, from voting to volunteering
civil disobedience = deliberately breaking a law, peacefully, to protest against it
grass-roots movement = a campaign started by ordinary people, not by parties or companies
solidarity = unity and mutual support among people with a shared goal
social justice = the idea that society should be fair in how it shares rights and resources
positive discrimination = giving extra help to a disadvantaged group to make opportunities fairer
congregation = a group of people who regularly worship together
multiculturalism = the view that different cultures can live together and keep their identities
UN = the United Nations, an international organisation for peace and cooperation
EU = the European Union, a political and economic union of European states
NATO = a military alliance of North American and European countries
humanitarian aid = food, medicine and shelter given to people in a crisis
sanctions = penalties, often economic, imposed on a country to change its behaviour
asylum seeker = a person who has applied for protection in another country and is waiting for a decision
refugee = a person who has fled their country because of war or persecution and been granted protection
member state = a country that belongs to an international organisation such as the EU
diplomatic relations = official political relations between countries
consular assistance = official help a country gives its citizens abroad
ambassador = the senior diplomat who represents a country abroad
peacekeeping = international military or civilian operations that help keep a ceasefire
ceasefire = an agreement to stop fighting for a period of time
economic migrant = a person who moves to another country mainly to work and improve their living standard
displaced person = someone forced to leave their home, often still inside their own country
deportation = forcing a person to leave a country by official order
development aid = money and expertise given to poorer countries to support long-term progress
developing country = a country with a lower average income and less industrialised economy
international law = rules that states have agreed should govern relations between them
freedom of religion = the right to hold, change or practise a faith, or to have none
place of worship = a building or site used for religious practice, such as a church, mosque or synagogue
separation of church and state = the principle that religious institutions should not run the government, and vice versa
